title: Batman: The Video Game
subtitle: Gotham as a platform challenge

body: Batman: The Video Game is Sunsoft’s NES action platformer tied to Tim Burton’s 1989 film. The route leads through Gotham’s streets, a chemical plant, sewers, a laboratory and the cathedral belltower toward the Joker. Sunsoft uses the licence as the setting for a demanding game of movement and combat, with only a loose connection to the film’s sequence of events. Batman’s compact sprite and the industrial stages put the emphasis on reading a space clearly and getting through it with controlled jumps.

Batman can jump away from a wall, letting the player climb shafts or change direction in the air. The ability gives level designers another surface to build around, so walls can be useful routes as well as boundaries. Reaching a platform may require a series of precise changes between facing directions. Enemies and hazards make those manoeuvres more demanding, because a safe landing depends on timing as well as height. The wall jump gives this version its own physical identity among the many games sharing the Batman name.

Fists handle close combat, while three projectile weapons offer different ways to attack from farther away. The batarang, batdisk and batpoon all draw on a supply of ammunition, making a difficult target a question of whether to spend it now. Bosses provide sharper tests of recognising an opening and choosing a response. Together with the wall jump, these options give the small action set enough variety to sustain the journey. The adaptation is remembered for what Batman can do in the player’s hands as much as for its film connection.
